analysis.investment_thesis: Cera is a fundamentally sound business with 10 consecutive years of positive earnings and near-zero debt, but at a P/E of 27.8x and P/B of 5.01x, the price demands far too much optimism for a value investor — the Graham Number (≈INR 2,135) sits at less than half the current price of INR 5,325, offering no margin of safety whatsoever. Mr. Market is pricing in a rosy future; I prefer to pay for a proven past at a discount.
key_strengths: 10-year unbroken earnings record: Net profit grew from INR 83 Cr (2016) to INR 249 Cr (2025) at 13% CAGR — exactly the kind of stability I demand.

Near-zero leverage: Debt/Equity of 0.04 and finance costs of just INR 7 Cr against operating income of INR 302 Cr gives an interest coverage of ~43x — the balance sheet can survive almost any downturn.
Positive operating cash flow all 5 of the last 5 years, with FCF consistently positive — earnings are real, not accounting fictions.
key_risks: Valuation is the primary risk: P/B of 5.01x means you are paying INR 5 for every INR 1 of net assets; any earnings disappointment or multiple compression could destroy capital rapidly.
Revenue growth is modest (8.6% CAGR over 9 years) and operating margins are thin (8.3%), leaving little buffer if input costs or competition intensify.
Operating cash flow halved in FY2025 (INR 122 Cr vs INR 236 Cr in FY2024) even as net profit grew — a divergence that warrants scrutiny of working capital management.
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ INR 2,135 vs market price INR 5,325 — stock trades at 2.5x intrinsic value by my measure.
P/E of 27.8x is nearly double my maximum threshold of 15x; combined P/E × P/B = 27.8 × 5.01 = 139, far exceeding my ceiling of 22.5.
FY2025 investing CF turned positive (+INR 127 Cr) while OCF fell to INR 122 Cr — likely asset monetisation, not organic cash generation strength.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Cera Sanitaryware passes every qualitative test I value: it has operated profitably for a full decade, carries trivial debt (borrowings of INR 67 Cr against equity of INR 1,354 Cr), and has never reported an annual loss in the data provided. ROCE of 22.4% and ROE of 18.2% demonstrate genuine capital efficiency. These are the hallmarks of a defensible, well-run business — the kind that deserves a place on a watch list. But deserving attention is not the same as deserving purchase at any price.

The arithmetic is damning. My Graham Number — the square root of (22.5 × EPS × Book Value Per Share) — yields approximately INR 2,135, using FY2025 net profit of INR 249 Cr and equity of INR 1,354 Cr across roughly 1.29 Cr shares. The market asks INR 5,325, a 150% premium to intrinsic value. A P/B of 5.0x and P/E of 27.8x leave no margin for error, no cushion against a slowdown in India's construction cycle, no protection if operating margins — already a slender 8.3% — compress further. The intelligent investor does not pay for hope; he pays for value. At INR 5,325, he is paying almost entirely for hope.
